stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and has 25 member accounts in several organizational units (OUs). The administrators of each member account have the AdministratorAccess policy and can edit the IAM policies of their account. Last month, one member account left the organization without approval, and the company lost its billing and security controls over that account. The company must ensure that no member account can leave the organization again. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: have the AdministratorAccess policy
ensure that no member account can leave
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Create an SCP that denies the organizations:LeaveOrganization action, and attach the SCP to the management account of the organization.
options.why: SCPs [affect only member accounts](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-no-effect-on-management-account), so an SCP on the management account does not limit the member accounts that could leave.

options.text: Create an SCP that denies the organizations:LeaveOrganization action, and attach the SCP to the root of the organization.
options.why: AWS recommends that you [attach an SCP at the root](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-deny-leave-and-close-recommended) that denies this action, and the Deny holds even when an administrator [attaches the AdministratorAccess IAM policy](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-admin-policy-cannot-override).

options.text: Create an SCP that denies the organizations:LeaveOrganization action, and attach the SCP directly to every member account as each account joins.
options.why: It works, but each new account needs one more attachment, and an SCP on the root is [enforced automatically in the newly added account](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-faq-policies-enforced-automatically-on-new-account).

options.text: Replace the AdministratorAccess policy in every member account with a customer managed policy that leaves out the organizations:LeaveOrganization action.
options.why: The administrators can add the action back to their IAM policies, but an SCP limits principals [including the member account's root user](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user).

explanation: Member accounts [can leave your organization or close themselves](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-deny-leave-and-close-recommended), so AWS recommends a Deny SCP on the root of the organization. One SCP on the root reaches every member account, new ones too. Principals in a member account [cannot remove or change SCPs that are applied to that account](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-faq-member-principals-cannot-change-scps), so the administrators cannot undo the control.
takeaway: To stop every member account from leaving, attach a Deny SCP to the root of the organization.
twin: If the stem said "a role in the management account must not delete a log group" instead: an SCP does not help, because SCPs have no effect on [users or roles in the management account](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-no-effect-on-management-account).
say: A Deny SCP on the root stops every member account from leaving, even with AdministratorAccess.

stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. To protect its logs, the security team attaches an SCP to the root of the organization. The SCP denies the logs:DeleteLogGroup action. A week later, an engineer signs in to the management account, uses an IAM role that has the AdministratorAccess policy, and deletes an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group in that account. The call succeeds. What is the reason that the call succeeds?
keywords: signs in to the management account
attaches an SCP to the root

options.text: The AdministratorAccess policy of the role overrides the Deny statement of the SCP.
options.why: In a member account the Deny wins even when an administrator [attaches the AdministratorAccess IAM policy](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-admin-policy-cannot-override), so the policy is not what makes this call succeed.

options.text: An SCP on the root applies to an account only after it is also attached to that account.
options.why: Policies such as an SCP on the root are [enforced automatically in the newly added account](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-faq-policies-enforced-automatically-on-new-account), without a second attachment to each account.
options.misconception: believes that an SCP on the root needs a second attachment on each account

options.text: SCPs do not restrict the users or roles in the management account of the organization.
options.why: SCPs [affect only member accounts](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-no-effect-on-management-account), so the role in the management account keeps every permission of its AdministratorAccess policy.

options.text: SCPs restrict the IAM users in an account but not the IAM roles in that account.
options.why: An SCP [restricts permissions for IAM users and roles in member accounts](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user), so roles are inside its scope.
options.misconception: believes that SCPs limit IAM users but not IAM roles

explanation: The SCP reaches every member account, but SCPs have no effect on [users or roles in the management account](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-no-effect-on-management-account). AWS gives this as the reason to store resources in other accounts and [keep them out of the management account](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-keep-resources-out-of-management-account).
takeaway: An SCP on the root limits the member accounts, not the management account.
twin: If the stem said "an engineer signs in to a member account" instead: the call fails, because the Deny holds even when an administrator [attaches the AdministratorAccess IAM policy](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-admin-policy-cannot-override).
say: SCPs skip the management account, so keep workloads out of it.

stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. The root of the organization has the FullAWSAccess SCP. In the Workloads organizational unit (OU), the company replaced FullAWSAccess with an allow-list SCP that allows only Amazon EC2, Amazon S3, and Amazon CloudWatch actions. One account in the Workloads OU now needs Amazon Athena. The account has FullAWSAccess attached directly, and the IAM role of its analytics team allows Athena actions. Every other account in the Workloads OU must keep the current allow list. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: allows only Amazon EC2, Amazon S3, and Amazon CloudWatch actions
Every other account in the Workloads OU must keep the current allow list
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Keep the account in the Workloads OU, and attach an SCP that allows Athena actions directly to the account, next to FullAWSAccess.
options.why: The Workloads OU still allows no Athena actions, and an Allow is needed [at every level from the root](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-allow-needed-at-every-level) through each OU to the account.

options.text: Keep the account in the Workloads OU, and add Athena actions to the allow-list SCP that is attached to the Workloads OU.
options.why: It gives the account Athena, but [accounts within the OU automatically inherit the policy](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-ou-policy-inherited-by-accounts), so the other Workloads accounts lose their current allow list.
options.misconception: overlooks that every account in an OU inherits a change to the SCP of the OU

options.text: Create a new account in a new OU whose SCPs allow Athena, and migrate the workloads and data of the account to the new account.
options.why: It works, but a migration is far more work, because AWS lets you [move accounts from one OU to another](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-ou-policy-inherited-by-accounts).

options.text: Create a new OU under the root with an SCP that allows Amazon EC2, Amazon S3, CloudWatch, and Athena, and move the account there.
options.why: The new path allows Athena at the root, at the new OU and at the account, and AWS lets you [move accounts from one OU to another](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-ou-policy-inherited-by-accounts).

explanation: SCP evaluation follows [a deny-by-default model](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-deny-by-default-model), and [there must be an explicit Allow statement](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-allow-needed-at-every-level) at the root, at each OU in the path and at the account. The Workloads OU allows no Athena actions, so the fix is a path without that OU. A new OU gives this one account Athena and leaves the other accounts unchanged.
takeaway: An Allow on the account does not help when an OU above it does not allow the action.
twin: If the stem said "every account in the Workloads OU needs Athena" instead: add Athena actions to the allow-list SCP of the Workloads OU, because [accounts within the OU automatically inherit the policy](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-ou-policy-inherited-by-accounts).

stem: A company runs its development, test, and production workloads in one AWS account. An audit finds that developers can change production resources. The company must isolate production from the other environments, keep its audit logs in a separate account, and apply the same security guardrails to every account that it creates in the future. The company does not have a multi-account environment yet. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: isolate production from the other environments
every account that it creates in the future
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Create an AWS Control Tower landing zone, and use Account Factory to create separate accounts for the production and non-production workloads.
options.why: Control Tower builds [a secure, compliant, multi-account AWS environment](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-easiest-way-secure-multi-account), and Account Factory is [a configurable account template](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-account-factory-template) that applies the same controls to each new account.

options.text: Keep one account, tag every resource with its environment, and use IAM policies with tag conditions and permissions boundaries to separate the teams.
options.why: An account provides [security, access, and billing boundaries](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-account-is-security-access-billing-boundary), and tags in one account keep production and the audit logs inside the same boundary.

options.text: Create an organization in AWS Organizations, create each account by hand, and deploy a security baseline to every account with AWS CloudFormation StackSets.
options.why: It works, but someone creates each account and maintains the baseline, and Account Factory [automates the process of applying controls and policies](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-account-factory-template).

options.text: Keep one account, and create a separate VPC for each environment, with no network path between the production VPC and the other VPCs.
options.why: A VPC separates network paths, not IAM permissions, so developers in the same account can still change production resources through the AWS APIs.
options.misconception: treats a VPC as a boundary for IAM permissions

explanation: Separate accounts isolate production: with separate accounts, [by default, the resources and data](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-separate-accounts-prod-nonprod-by-default) of one environment are separated from the others. A Control Tower landing zone provisions [the log archive account, and the audit account](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-shared-accounts) during its setup. Account Factory then gives each new account the same controls.
takeaway: Isolation, a separate log account and guardrails for future accounts point to a Control Tower landing zone.
twin: If the stem said "keep one account and limit who can change production resources" instead: IAM policies with tag conditions can meet it, because the stem no longer asks for separate accounts.
say: Separate accounts isolate production, and Control Tower gives every new account the same guardrails.

stem: A company has 12 AWS accounts. Each account receives its own bill, and each team owns one or more of the accounts. The finance team wants one bill for all accounts, volume pricing that is based on the combined usage of all accounts, and a monthly cost report for each team. Every team already tags its resources with a team tag. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: one bill for all accounts
a monthly cost report for each team
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Create an organization in AWS Organizations from one account, and invite the other accounts to join the organization.
options.why: The management account is [responsible for paying all charges](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-management-account-pays-all-charges), and AWS treats the accounts [as if they were one account](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-billing-treats-accounts-as-one-for-tiers) for billing.

options.text: Activate the team tag as a user-defined cost allocation tag in the Billing console of each member account.
options.why: [Only the management account in an organization](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-cost-allocation-tags-management-account) has access to the cost allocation tags manager, so member accounts cannot activate the tag.
options.misconception: believes that each member account activates its own cost allocation tags

options.text: Create an organization, create 12 new member accounts in it, and migrate the workloads of each team into the new accounts.
options.why: It works, but existing accounts can join by invitation, so new accounts and a migration add work and give no extra benefit.

options.text: Activate the team tag as a user-defined cost allocation tag in the Billing console of the management account.
options.why: [Only the management account in an organization](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-cost-allocation-tags-management-account) has access to the cost allocation tags manager, and the activated tag splits the costs by team.

options.text: Attach an SCP to the root of the organization that allows the billing and cost management actions for every team.
options.why: [An SCP never grants permissions](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-never-grants-permissions), and the bill and the tag reports do not depend on the permissions of the teams.

explanation: Consolidated billing gives one bill: the management account pays, and [AWS combines the usage from all accounts](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-billing-treats-accounts-as-one-for-tiers) to decide the volume pricing tiers. A report per team needs the team tag as a cost allocation tag, and the management account activates it. Inviting the existing accounts keeps their workloads where they are.
takeaway: One bill and combined pricing come from an organization; team reports come from a tag activated in the management account.
twin: If the stem said "each team must keep a separate bill" instead: one organization does not fit, because AWS treats its accounts [as if they were one account](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-billing-treats-accounts-as-one-for-tiers) for billing.
say: One organization gives one bill and combined pricing, and the management account activates the team tag.

stem: A company uses AWS Organizations. Administrators in the management account manage member accounts by assuming the OrganizationAccountAccessRole IAM role in each account. Last month, the company invited an existing AWS account that another business unit used before, and the account accepted the invitation. When an administrator tries to assume OrganizationAccountAccessRole in the invited account, the request fails. What is the reason for the failure?
keywords: invited an existing AWS account
assume OrganizationAccountAccessRole in the invited account

options.text: An SCP on the root of the organization blocks the management account from assuming roles in member accounts.
options.why: SCPs [affect only member accounts](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-no-effect-on-management-account), so they do not limit the administrator in the management account who makes the call.

options.text: Organizations creates this role only in accounts that it creates, not in accounts that join by invitation.
options.why: When Organizations creates an account, it [automatically creates an IAM role](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-created-account-gets-access-role); if the account was invited, [Organizations did not automatically create such a role](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-invited-account-access-role-optional).

options.text: The role is created in an invited account only after an administrator moves the account into an OU.
options.why: The OU decides which policies the account inherits, and for an invited account [Organizations did not automatically create such a role](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-invited-account-access-role-optional) in any OU.
options.misconception: believes that moving an account into an OU creates the access role

options.text: The role is created in an invited account only after the account approves the request to enable all features.
options.why: Approval changes the feature set of the organization, but it creates no role; after the account accepts, an administrator can [choose to create an IAM role](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-invited-account-access-role-optional).
options.misconception: believes that approving all features creates the access role

explanation: Organizations [automatically creates an IAM role](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-created-account-gets-access-role) named OrganizationAccountAccessRole in an account that it creates. An invited account is different: after it accepts, an administrator can [choose to create an IAM role](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-invited-account-access-role-optional) that lets the management account access it. The fix is to create that role in the invited account with a trust policy that names the management account.
takeaway: Created accounts get OrganizationAccountAccessRole; in an invited account, an administrator creates the role.
twin: If the stem said "an account that the organization created" instead: the role exists, because Organizations [automatically creates an IAM role](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-created-account-gets-access-role) there, so check the trust policy and the caller's IAM policy.
say: Invited accounts do not get OrganizationAccountAccessRole, so an administrator creates it.

stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. The company stores confidential data in Amazon S3 buckets in many member accounts, and teams create new buckets every week. A security review adds a new rule: principals in the company's accounts must not access S3 buckets that belong to other AWS organizations. The rule must apply to every current and future member account. Which solution will restrict this access with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: principals in the company's accounts
buckets that belong to other AWS organizations
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Attach a service control policy (SCP) to the root that denies Amazon S3 actions unless the bucket belongs to the company's organization, based on the aws:ResourceOrgID condition key.
options.why: SCPs [control which resources your identities can access](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-controls-which-resources-identities-access), so one Deny on the root keeps the principals of every member account away from outside buckets.

options.text: Attach a resource control policy (RCP) to the root that denies Amazon S3 actions unless the principal belongs to the company's organization, based on the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key.
options.why: RCPs [affect only resources](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-rcp-applies-to-own-resources-even-external-callers) that accounts of the organization manage, so the buckets of other organizations are outside the scope of the RCP.
options.misconception: believes that an RCP limits what the company's own principals do with the resources of other companies

options.text: Set a permissions boundary on every IAM role in every member account that denies Amazon S3 actions on buckets that belong to other organizations.
options.why: It can work for IAM roles, but each new role in each new account needs the boundary, which is far more work than one SCP.

options.text: Add a statement to the bucket policy of every S3 bucket in every member account that denies access to principals outside the company's organization.
options.why: A bucket policy controls who can reach that bucket, so it does not stop the company's principals from reaching buckets of other organizations.
options.misconception: believes that a policy on the company's own buckets limits where the company's principals can go

explanation: The rule limits what the company's own principals can reach. SCPs [control which resources your identities can access](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-controls-which-resources-identities-access), and one SCP on the root covers every current and future member account. RCPs work in the other direction: they [control which identities can access your resources](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-controls-which-resources-identities-access).
takeaway: Your principals to outside resources: an SCP. Outside principals to your resources: an RCP.
twin: If the stem said "principals outside the company's organization must not access the company's S3 buckets, even when a bucket policy allows them" instead: the RCP, because RCPs [control which identities can access your resources](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-controls-which-resources-identities-access).

stem: A company uses AWS Control Tower to govern its accounts in AWS Organizations. The security team finds that some teams create accounts with the AWS Organizations CreateAccount API in an organizational unit (OU) that is not registered with Control Tower. The controls of the landing zone do not apply to these accounts. The company must make sure that every future account gets the landing zone controls automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: that is not registered with Control Tower
every future account gets the landing zone controls automatically
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Turn on more detective controls in the landing zone, so that the controls also apply to the accounts in the OU that is not registered.
options.why: New OUs or accounts created outside Control Tower stay outside its controls until you [separately register the OU or enroll the account](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-accounts-outside-not-bound), whatever the landing zone turns on.

options.text: Use an Amazon EventBridge rule and an AWS Lambda function that copy the control SCPs and AWS Config rules to each account that CreateAccount creates.
options.why: It can work, but the company then writes and maintains custom code that repeats what registration and Account Factory do.

options.text: Register the OU with AWS Control Tower, enroll the existing accounts of the OU, and create every new account with Account Factory.
options.why: Controls apply after you [separately register the OU or enroll the account](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-accounts-outside-not-bound), and Account Factory [automates the process of applying controls and policies](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-account-factory-template) to each new account.

options.text: Deploy AWS Config rules that match the landing zone controls to the OU with AWS CloudFormation StackSets and automatic deployment to new accounts.
options.why: [Detective controls are implemented using AWS Config rules](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-control-types-mechanisms), so the rules report changes and do not bring the preventive controls of the landing zone.

explanation: The OU is outside Control Tower governance, and new accounts created outside Account Factory [are not bound by the registered OU's controls](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-accounts-outside-not-bound). The fix has two parts. Registration brings the OU and its accounts under the controls, and Account Factory is [a configurable account template](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-account-factory-template) that applies the controls to every new account.
takeaway: Control Tower governs registered OUs and enrolled accounts; create new accounts with Account Factory.
twin: If the stem said "teams create accounts with CreateAccount in a registered OU" instead: enroll those accounts and use Account Factory, because accounts created outside it [are not bound by the registered OU's controls](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-accounts-outside-not-bound).

stem: A company uses AWS Control Tower. The accounts in the Workloads organizational unit (OU) hold Amazon S3 buckets that store audit logs. Developers in these accounts deploy changes with the AWS Management Console and the AWS CLI. The company must prevent every principal in the Workloads OU accounts from deleting the audit log buckets. An alert after a deletion is not enough. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: must prevent every principal
An alert after a deletion is not enough
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Turn on a detective control for the Workloads OU in AWS Control Tower, so that an AWS Config rule reports the deletion of the audit log buckets.
options.why: [Detective controls detect specific events when they occur](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-preventive-detective-proactive-defined), so the bucket is already gone when the alert arrives.

options.text: Turn on a proactive control for the Workloads OU in AWS Control Tower, so that a CloudFormation hook checks the deletion of the audit log buckets.
options.why: Proactive controls check resources [by means of CloudFormation stack operations](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-proactive-only-cloudformation), so a deletion from the console or the CLI does not pass through the check.
options.misconception: believes that a proactive control checks every request, also console and CLI calls

options.text: Create an SCP that denies the deletion of the audit log buckets, and attach the SCP in AWS Organizations to each account of the Workloads OU.
options.why: It works, but each account needs its own attachment, and each new account in the OU needs one more step.

options.text: Turn on a preventive control for the Workloads OU in AWS Control Tower, so that an SCP denies the deletion of the audit log buckets.
options.why: [Preventive controls prevent actions from occurring](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-preventive-detective-proactive-defined), so the deletion fails in every account of the OU, from the console and from the CLI.

explanation: The verb is prevent. [Preventive controls prevent actions from occurring](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-preventive-detective-proactive-defined), and Control Tower implements them with Service Control Policies (SCPs), [Resource Control Policies (RCPs), and declarative policies](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-control-types-mechanisms). One control on the OU reaches each account of the OU. A detective control reports after the event, and a proactive control checks CloudFormation stack operations.
takeaway: Prevent points to a preventive control, which is an SCP. Detect points to a detective control, which is an AWS Config rule.
twin: If the stem said "must receive an alert when an audit log bucket is deleted" instead: a detective control, because [detective controls detect specific events when they occur](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-preventive-detective-proactive-defined).
say: To stop the deletion, turn on a preventive control on the OU; a detective control only reports it.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
I mark the constraints: the company must prevent the deletion, an alert after the deletion is not enough, and developers use the console and the CLI.
Before I look at the options, I predict a preventive control on the Workloads OU, because preventive controls prevent actions from occurring.

I remove the detective control, because it detects the event when it occurs, and then the bucket is already gone. I remove the proactive control, because it checks CloudFormation stack operations, and the developers use the console and the CLI.
Between the preventive control on the OU and the SCP on each account, the difference is the work per account; the stem asks for the LEAST operational overhead, so one control on the OU wins.
Check: the preventive control on the OU stops the deletion from the console and the CLI in every account of the OU, and it needs no step per account. Time: 90 seconds.

stem: A company uses AWS Organizations. A network team uses a network account to centrally manage one VPC, including the route tables and the NAT gateways. Application teams in six other accounts of the organization must launch Amazon EC2 instances into subnets of this VPC. Each team must own its instances in its own account. The network team must keep full control of the route tables and the NAT gateways. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: launch Amazon EC2 instances into subnets of this VPC
own its instances in its own account
keep full control of the route tables
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Share the subnets of the VPC with the six application accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).
options.why: In a shared subnet, [participants cannot work with route tables](../facts/ram.md#ram-vpc-participants-no-route-tables-nat), so routing stays with the network team, and RAM [eliminates the need to provision duplicate resources](../facts/ram.md#ram-reduces-overhead-no-duplicate-resources).

options.text: Share the subnets of the VPC with the IAM roles of the application teams through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).
options.why: RAM can share subnets with [only AWS accounts in its own organization](../facts/ram.md#ram-share-subnets-only-within-organization), not with IAM roles or IAM users.

options.text: Create a VPC in each application account, connect each VPC to the central VPC with VPC peering, and manage the routes through a cross-account role.
options.why: It works, but six VPCs, peering connections and a cross-account role are far more to run than one shared VPC.

options.text: Create an IAM role in the network account that the application teams assume to launch their instances into the subnets of the VPC.
options.why: Instances launched through a role in the network account belong to the network account, so the teams do not own them in their own accounts.
options.misconception: believes that an instance launched through an assumed role belongs to the account of the caller

explanation: AWS RAM shares the subnets of one VPC with other accounts of the organization, and each team launches instances into the shared subnets from its own account. [Participants cannot work with route tables](../facts/ram.md#ram-vpc-participants-no-route-tables-nat), and [participants cannot create, delete, or describe NAT gateways](../facts/ram.md#ram-vpc-participants-no-route-tables-nat), so the network team keeps that control.
takeaway: Many accounts in one centrally managed VPC: share the subnets with AWS RAM.
twin: If the stem said "partner companies outside the organization" instead: subnet sharing does not fit, because RAM shares subnets with [only AWS accounts in its own organization](../facts/ram.md#ram-share-subnets-only-within-organization).
say: Share the subnets with AWS RAM; the teams launch into them, and the network team keeps the routing.

stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. The company stores confidential data in Amazon S3 buckets in many member accounts, and teams create new buckets every week. A security review adds a new rule: principals outside the company's organization must not access the company's S3 buckets, even when a bucket policy allows them. The rule must apply to every current and future member account. Which solution will restrict this access with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: principals outside the company's organization
even when a bucket policy allows them
LEAST operational overhead

options.text: Attach a service control policy (SCP) to the root that denies Amazon S3 actions unless the bucket belongs to the company's organization, based on the aws:ResourceOrgID condition key.
options.why: SCPs [do not affect users or roles from accounts outside the organization](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-not-outside-principals-or-resource-policies), so a bucket policy can still let them in.

options.text: Attach a resource control policy (RCP) to the root that denies Amazon S3 actions unless the principal belongs to the company's organization, based on the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key.
options.why: RCPs [control which identities can access your resources](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-controls-which-resources-identities-access), and a bucket under a blocking RCP [does not have that permission](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-rcp-resource-policy-cannot-override), even if its bucket policy allows full access.

options.text: Set a permissions boundary on every IAM role in every member account that denies Amazon S3 actions on buckets that belong to other organizations.
options.why: A permissions boundary limits the company's own IAM roles, and principals from other organizations do not carry a boundary from the company.
options.misconception: believes that a boundary on the company's roles also limits principals from other organizations

options.text: Add a statement to the bucket policy of every S3 bucket in every member account that denies access to principals outside the company's organization.
options.why: It works, but every new bucket needs the statement, and teams create new buckets every week.

explanation: The rule limits who can reach the company's buckets, and the callers come from outside. [SCPs can only impact the effective permissions](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-rcp-affects-external-principals-scp-only-internal) of principals inside the organization. RCPs reach [principals external to your organization](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-rcp-affects-external-principals-scp-only-internal), and one RCP on the root covers the buckets of every current and future member account.
takeaway: Outside principals reaching the company's buckets: an RCP on the root, not an SCP.
twin: If the stem said "principals in the company's accounts must not access S3 buckets that belong to other AWS organizations" instead: the SCP, because SCPs [control which resources your identities can access](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-controls-which-resources-identities-access).

stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and adds new member accounts every month. A network team uses a network account to centrally manage Amazon Route 53 Resolver rules that every account must use, including future accounts. An administrator turned on trusted access for AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) in the AWS Organizations console. When the administrator tries to share the rules with the whole organization, the share fails. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?
keywords: adds new member accounts every month
turned on trusted access for AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) in the AWS Organizations console
MOST operationally efficient

options.text: Share the Resolver rules with the account ID of each member account, and ask each account to accept the invitation that AWS RAM sends.
options.why: It works, because Resolver rules [can share with any AWS account](../facts/ram.md#ram-share-resolver-rules-any-account), but each new account needs another share entry and another invitation.

options.text: Add a resource-based policy to the Resolver rules that lists the account ID of every member account, and update the policy for each new account.
options.why: RAM can share with the organization without the need to [enumerate every one of the AWS account IDs](../facts/ram.md#ram-vs-resource-policy-org-ou-without-ids), so a list of accounts adds work every month.
options.misconception: believes that a resource-based policy that lists accounts is the way to share with a whole organization

options.text: Enable sharing with AWS Organizations in the AWS RAM console, and then share the Resolver rules with the organization in one resource share.
options.why: To share in the organization, [you must first use the AWS RAM console](../facts/ram.md#ram-org-sharing-no-invitations) or the CLI to enable sharing; then one share names the whole organization.

options.text: Attach an SCP to the root of the organization that allows all AWS RAM actions, and then share the Resolver rules with the organization again.
options.why: [An SCP never grants permissions](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-never-grants-permissions), and the share fails because sharing with AWS Organizations is not enabled in AWS RAM.

explanation: The setting was turned on in the wrong place. [You must enable sharing with AWS Organizations](../facts/ram.md#ram-enable-sharing-in-ram-console-not-orgs) by using the AWS RAM console or the AWS CLI, because trusted access from the AWS Organizations console does not create the RAM service-linked role. Inside the organization, AWS RAM then sends no invitations, and a share with the whole organization [counts as only one against this quota](../facts/ram.md#ram-whole-organization-counts-as-one-principal).
takeaway: Enable sharing with AWS Organizations in the AWS RAM console, then share once with the organization.
twin: If the stem said "partner companies outside the organization must use the rules" instead: share with each partner account ID, because Resolver rules [can share with any AWS account](../facts/ram.md#ram-share-resolver-rules-any-account).
